name: Norman Foster
bio:
Norman Foster (born 1935) is an English architect and a pioneer of high-tech architecture, known for steel-and-glass buildings whose structure shapes the design. He founded Foster Associates in 1967, now Foster + Partners, and won the Pritzker Prize in 1999.

His early buildings, the Willis Building in Ipswich (1975) and the Sainsbury Centre for Visual Arts in Norwich (1978), tried out open-plan floors on a clear structural grid behind glass walls. The HSBC Main Building in Hong Kong hangs its floors from steel masts and trusses, built from large modules made in Britain and shipped out. The Commerzbank Tower in Frankfurt (1997) is often called the first ecological skyscraper, with sky gardens that bring daylight and fresh air into the offices. In Berlin, Foster rebuilt the Reichstag (1999) for the German parliament and topped it with a walk-in glass dome. With the engineer Michel Virlogeux he designed the Millau Viaduct (2004), and in London he built 30 St Mary Axe (2004). Foster's projects are studied for how structure, daylight and energy use can drive the form of a building.

name: Renzo Piano
bio:
Renzo Piano (born 1937) is an Italian architect from Genoa, known for carefully engineered buildings and for museums lit by daylight from above. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1998, and his practice is the Renzo Piano Building Workshop.

Piano became known with the Centre Pompidou in Paris (1977), designed with Richard Rogers as an "inside-out" building, with its structure, pipes and escalators on the outside. His later projects are quieter. The Menil Collection in Houston (1987) was built to make the most of natural light, and the Fondation Beyeler near Basel (1997) has a glass roof that lets in north light and screens out the east and west sun. The Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural Centre in Nouméa (1998) lines up ten curved timber "cases" along a ridge, patterned on the great huts of the Kanak people and tested in wind tunnels for ventilation. Kansai International Airport Terminal 1 in Osaka (1994) stands on an artificial island, and The Shard in London (2012), 305 metres tall, was Europe's tallest skyscraper when it was finished. Renzo Piano's buildings are studied for their details, their use of daylight, and their response to place.

name: Oscar Niemeyer
bio:
Oscar Niemeyer (1907–2012) was a Brazilian architect and a key figure of modern architecture, known for free, flowing curves in reinforced concrete. He designed the main civic buildings of Brasília, the planned city that became Brazil's capital in 1960, and won the Pritzker Prize in 1988.

Niemeyer said his architecture really began at Pampulha, near Belo Horizonte, where the Church of Saint Francis of Assisi (1943) is built from parabolic concrete arches. He worked with Lúcio Costa on the Gustavo Capanema Palace in Rio de Janeiro, and with Le Corbusier and others on the United Nations Secretariat Building in New York. The Copan Building in São Paulo wraps its apartments in a long, wavy façade. In Brasília, the National Congress of Brazil sets two half-spheres, one for each chamber, beside twin office towers, and the Cathedral of Brasília rises as a ring of sixteen curved concrete columns with glass between them. At 89 he designed the Niterói Contemporary Art Museum (1996), a saucer on a cylindrical base above the bay. Oscar Niemeyer's buildings show students how far concrete can be shaped.

name: Zaha Hadid
bio:
Zaha Hadid (1950–2016) was an Iraqi-British architect whose buildings broke with straight-edged modernism, first through sharp, tilting planes and later through long, flowing curves. Born in Baghdad and trained at the Architectural Association in London, she used painting as a design tool, was shown in the 1988 "Deconstructivism in Architecture" exhibition at New York's Museum of Modern Art, and in 2004 became the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize.

Her first built project, the Vitra Fire Station in Weil am Rhein (1993), is made of angled planes of exposed concrete. The Phaeno Science Center in Wolfsburg (2005) lifts a concrete building onto ten hollow cones, each holding a room, leaving open space beneath. MAXXI in Rome (2010) won the Stirling Prize. The London Aquatics Centre (2011), built for the 2012 Olympics, has a wave-like roof that Hadid said was inspired by moving water. The Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku (2012) folds the ground into one continuous surface and avoids straight lines altogether. Zaha Hadid's projects are studied for the way new forms and their structure were invented together.

name: Le Corbusier
bio:
Le Corbusier (1887–1965), born Charles-Édouard Jeanneret in Switzerland and a French citizen from 1930, was an architect, urban planner, painter and writer, and one of the pioneers of modern architecture. In 2016, seventeen of his projects in seven countries were listed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Villa Savoye in Poissy (1931) sums up his Five Points of Architecture: the house stands on pilotis, with a free plan, a free façade, ribbon windows and a roof garden. After the Second World War, the Unité d'Habitation in Marseille (1952) stacked two-level flats along interior "streets" in rough-cast concrete, béton brut, and is often named as the first inspiration for brutalism. Notre-Dame du Haut at Ronchamp (1955) has thick curved walls under a concrete roof shell, with daylight entering through a thin gap and deep, scattered windows. Sainte-Marie de La Tourette near Lyon (1960) is measured with his Modulor, a system of proportions based on the human body. He also planned the city of Chandigarh and its Capitol Complex. Le Corbusier's buildings and books remain a starting point for students, though his politics and city plans are still debated.

name: Alvar Aalto
bio:
Alvar Aalto (1898–1976) was a Finnish architect and designer who gave modernism a human scale through wood, brick, daylight and curving lines. His career runs from Nordic Classicism in the 1920s, through functionalism in the 1930s, to the organic modernism of his later work. With his first wife, Aino Aalto, he also designed furniture, lamps and glassware, and their bent plywood furniture influenced Charles and Ray Eames.

The Paimio Sanatorium (1933), designed with Aino Aalto, and Viipuri Library in Vyborg (1935) first won him world attention; the library has an undulating timber ceiling shaped to spread sound and deep round skylights that light the reading desks without glare. At Villa Mairea in Noormarkku (1939), stair columns of bound wood suggest a forest. Baker House at MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts (1949), bends along the Charles River to give each room a view and fresh air, and began his red-brick period. Säynätsalo Town Hall (1952) gathers a council chamber, offices and a library around a raised courtyard in brick, timber and copper. Alvar Aalto's buildings are studied for natural materials, daylight, and designing a building and its furnishings as one.

name: Frank Gehry
bio:
Frank Gehry (1929–2025) was a Canadian-American architect, born in Toronto and based in Los Angeles, known for sculptural buildings of curving metal and for using everyday materials in unexpected ways. His work is often called deconstructivist, a label he resisted, and he won the Pritzker Prize in 1989.

His own house, the Gehry Residence in Santa Monica (1978), wrapped an ordinary house in corrugated steel, chain-link fencing and plywood while leaving the old walls visible. The Guggenheim Bilbao (1997), clad in titanium, gave its name to the "Bilbao effect": one building helping to revive a city's economy. To build the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles (2003), with its stainless steel skin, his office used CATIA, software made for designing fighter jets. The Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris (2014) wraps its galleries in twelve glass "sails". Gehry was one of the first architects to see what computer design could do, and his projects show students how software can turn a complex sketch into a buildable form.

name: Herzog & de Meuron
bio:
Herzog & de Meuron is a Swiss architecture practice founded in Basel in 1978 by Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron, known for inventive use of materials and for turning old structures to new uses. The two founders shared the Pritzker Prize in 2001, and the firm has worked on more than 600 projects in 40 countries.

Tate Modern in London (2000) turned the Bankside Power Station into a museum, keeping the vast Turbine Hall and adding a two-storey glass extension on the roof. The Allianz Arena in Munich (2005) is wrapped in inflated ETFE plastic panels that can be lit from inside, the first stadium with a façade that changes colour. The Beijing National Stadium (2008), the "Bird's Nest", hides the supports of its roof in a web of steel beams around a concrete seating bowl, with the artist Ai Weiwei as consultant. The Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg (2017) sets a glass concert hall with a wave-shaped roofline on top of a brick warehouse. Students study Herzog & de Meuron's projects for their inventive façades and their reuse of existing buildings.

name: OMA
bio:
OMA, the Office for Metropolitan Architecture, is an architecture practice founded in 1975 by Rem Koolhaas, Elia Zenghelis, Madelon Vriesendorp and Zoe Zenghelis. Based in Rotterdam, with offices in New York, Hong Kong, Doha and Australia, it began with unbuilt "paper" projects about Manhattan, the subject of Koolhaas's book Delirious New York. Koolhaas, often linked with deconstructivism, won the Pritzker Prize in 2000.

The Kunsthal in Rotterdam (1992) was one of OMA's early buildings to win critical attention. The Seattle Central Library (2004) stacks a set of "floating platforms" inside a steel net and glass skin; its "Books Spiral" keeps the non-fiction collection on one continuous run instead of breaking it up across floors. Casa da Música in Porto (2005) is a nine-storey polyhedron clad in white concrete and cut by large windows. The CCTV Headquarters in Beijing (2012) joins two leaning towers into a loop of six sections with an open centre. Students read OMA's buildings together with Koolhaas's writing, from Delirious New York to S,M,L,XL, which argues about the modern city as much as about buildings.

name: Glenn Murcutt
bio:
Glenn Murcutt (born 1936) is an Australian architect known for houses shaped by their landscape and climate. Born in London to Australian parents, he spent his first years in Papua New Guinea, where he first met vernacular building. He works alone, without staff, builds only in Australia, and won the Pritzker Prize in 2002, the only Australian to do so.

His motto, "touch the earth lightly", means studying a site's wind, water, temperature and light before drawing the building. His houses use glass, stone, timber, concrete, steel and corrugated iron. The Marie Short House near Kempsey (1975) and the Magney House at Bingie Point (1984) are among his best-known homes. The Arthur and Yvonne Boyd Education Centre at Riversdale (1999), designed with Wendy Lewin and Reg Lark, sits on a rise; the critic Philip Drew compared its hall to an ancient Greek temple, roofed in corrugated iron. Glenn Murcutt's projects are studied for climate-led design at the scale of a house.
